clinicalPearls: Near-constant or frequent abdominal pain that is poorly related to eating, defecation or menstruation
The pain reflects central amplification of visceral signals rather than a gut-based trigger
It is often associated with loss of daily function and with psychological comorbidity
There may be behavioural clues such as the closed-eyes sign and a discrepancy between reported severity and examination
It is distinct from irritable bowel syndrome, in which pain is linked to bowel function
Management centres on a therapeutic relationship, central neuromodulators and psychological therapies rather than repeated investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome arises from dysregulation of central pain processing, in which descending pain-modulatory pathways fail to dampen, and instead amplify, visceral afferent input. This central sensitisation means pain is experienced largely independently of gut events. Psychological factors and prior experiences influence the pain through the gut-brain axis, and repeated negative investigations and escalating analgesia, particularly opioids, can perpetuate the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic pancreatitis or other structural abdominal disease
Abdominal wall pain (for example nerve entrapment)
additionalInvestigations: Focused history and examination, including the Carnett test for abdominal wall pain
Limited, targeted testing to exclude structural disease rather than repeated investigation
Assessment of psychological comorbidity and functional impact
Review of analgesic, especially opioid, use
Consideration of prior imaging to avoid duplication
redFlags: New alarm features such as weight loss, bleeding or a mass
Escalating opioid use with worsening pain
Features suggesting a specific structural disease
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic, but a supportive clinician relationship with neuromodulator and psychological treatment can substantially reduce pain and improve function; repeated testing and opioids worsen outcomes.
pitfalls: Repeated investigation and surgery in search of a structural cause
Escalating opioids and precipitating narcotic bowel syndrome
Missing abdominal wall pain, which the Carnett test can identify
Failing to address psychological and gut-brain contributors
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Establish a strong, continuous therapeutic clinician-patient relationship as the foundation of care
Prescribe central neuromodulators as the mainstay, such as tricyclic antidepressants or serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors
Offer psychological therapies including cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy
Wean and avoid opioids, which perpetuate the syndrome through narcotic bowel
Limit repeated investigations and set realistic goals focused on restoring daily function
Escalate to a specialist gastroenterology or multidisciplinary pain service for refractory pain
